properties.Name: I-95
properties.WhyShort: I-95 was built in the middle of Jackson Ward cutting it in half and disrupting many homes and businesses.
properties.WhyLong: In the 1950s, I-95 bisected Second Street and Jackson Ward as a whole. A block wide path was carved through the ward displacing an estimated 1,000 households and destroying hundreds of historic homes, buildings, and neighborhood structures. With construction ending in 1958, disruptions to the neighborhood were far from over. Today, about 150,000 cars per day drive along this portion of I-95 creating constant noise pollution. Along with this, the Northern section of Jackson Ward continues to be cut off from Historic Jackson Ward with less access to businesses and services.

properties.Name: Slaughter's Hotel
properties.WhyShort: The hotel was seen as an important hub for Black community and civil rights groups.
properties.WhyLong: Slaughter’s Hotel was first opened by Richard Slaughter around 1924. By 1931 the hotel moved to a larger location across the street. Slaughter’s was well known for its dedication to high quality food and accommodations for Black travelers at a time when options were limited. From the 1930s-1940s the hotel was a prominent establishment that attracted lots of notable guests such as Oliver Hill. Gertrude Taylor took over hotel management in 1945 after Richard Slaughter passed away. Under Taylor’s management the hotel thrived as a gathering place for organizations such as the NAACP and the Richmond Crusade of Voters. Along with this, the hotel also served as a meeting place for political, social, and community leaders. Through the 1970s the hotel continued to be a staple with its club sandwich becoming a local legend. In the early 1990s the hotel was demolished to make way for the Jackson Center.

properties.Name: Hotel Eggleston
properties.WhyShort: The hotel served as a gathering place for the civil rights community, performers, and Black travelers.
properties.WhyLong: In 1942, Neverett A. Eggleston Sr. purchased Hotel Eggleston. Having amenities like a grill, dining room, and pool room the hotel became a staple. During World War 2, the hotel was a bustling business that catered to both locals and visiting celebrities such as Billie Holiday and Joe Louis. Hotel Eggleston became part of the fabric of Jackson Ward serving as a gathering place for the civil rights community, performers, and Black travelers. The hotel was a notable stop for Black travelers as it boasted modern amenities such as 24 hour food service and air conditioned rooms. Due to integration in the 1970s, the hotel’s success started to dwindle as people started to move away for new opportunities. By the 1980s the hotel was vacant.

properties.Name: Club 533
properties.WhyShort: A club for Richmond's Black Professional and Businessmen that became a space for meetings, social events, and fostering relationships.
properties.WhyLong: Founded in 1956 by a group of men with interests in improving the social and civic welfare of citizens in Richmond, Club 533 served as an organization for Richmond’s Black Professional and Businessmen. The club fostered relationships among local African American professionals, spaces for meetings, civic engagement, and social events. Along with this, the club also helped improve the community's well-being through hosting different initiatives such as educational workshops and holiday parties. Club 533 has played a large role in the revitalization and historical significance of Jackson Ward.
